profiles.meeting_scenario: A hospital-affiliated rehabilitation innovation team is holding a design review for a nearly finalized pilot program that will let stroke and orthopedic outpatients use commercial video games with adapted motion controllers as a home supplement to standard therapy. The proposal includes a game-selection rubric, a therapist setup workflow, weekly progress summaries, and a four-week take-home kit. The meeting agenda is to review whether the current pilot design is ready for internal approval, identify any missing modifications, and confirm what will be included in the first pilot release. The expected outcome is a decision to approve the pilot with minor revisions and assign final follow-up actions.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Neurologic physical therapy, outpatient stroke rehabilitation, therapy dosing and home-exercise adherence
members.background: Lena is a senior physical therapist who has led several hospital pilots translating research tools into routine outpatient rehabilitation workflows, especially for upper-limb recovery after stroke.
members.private_state: She wants the design review to end with conditional approval so the pilot can start this quarter, and she is quietly worried that if the design feels operationally heavy, clinic managers will delay or cancel it.
hidden_assumptions: When a rehab supplement is described as 'safe for home use,' therapist screening and the standard home-program precautions are assumed rather than re-specified in the design packet.
A 'weekly progress summary' is primarily for the treating therapist to quickly judge whether prescribed movement practice is happening and whether the patient stayed engaged enough to continue.
If the proposal says the pilot is 'ready,' it means clinically workable with minor documentation gaps, not fully locked for every downstream operational detail.
The 'starter game set' naturally means the three commercial games already tested informally in her clinic lab with adapted shoulder and reach motions.
A home setup step that is 'remote' is ordinarily done through the hospital's existing tele-rehab video visit workflow, even if the document does not name the platform.

members.name: Evan Cho
members.expertise: Game interaction design, adapted controllers, patient-facing onboarding flows, engagement instrumentation
members.background: Evan came from a digital therapeutics startup and now supports the hospital's cross-disciplinary rehab technology projects, translating clinical goals into usable gameplay systems and dashboards.
members.private_state: He wants the review to preserve a clean, scalable product structure that can later be reused across clinics, and he is quietly concerned that ad hoc therapist customization will create inconsistent data and support burdens.
hidden_assumptions: When a system is labeled 'safe for home use,' the package itself should prevent foreseeable misuse through built-in calibration limits, on-screen guidance, and clear self-serve fail states rather than relying mainly on clinician judgment.

A 'weekly progress summary' should be a standardized patient-facing and admin-shareable report showing session completion, calibrated range achieved, and game challenge progression in a comparable format.
If the proposal is 'ready,' it means implementation-complete enough that support, handoff, and replication details are settled, because those are expensive to retrofit later.

The 'starter game set' means the three titles listed in the current slide deck that he selected for their configurable difficulty and telemetry hooks, including one rhythm game not used in Lena's informal lab trials.
A 'remote' setup implies an asynchronous onboarding path using the kit's mobile instructions and automated calibration flow, with live video only as an exception.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the weekly progress summary
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss providing a 'weekly progress summary.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a brief therapist-oriented note showing adherence to prescribed movement practice, rough tolerance, and whether the patient should stay on the same games next week.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a standardized dashboard/report artifact with engagement, calibration, and progression metrics suitable for patients, therapists, and program administrators.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see summaries as obviously useful and neither expects the other to mean anything radically different because 'progress summary' sounds like a settled, ordinary deliverable in pilot materials.

misalignment_points.topic: Which game bundle is the starter set
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to approving the 'starter game set' for the first pilot cohort.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the three commercial games her clinic staff already used in mock sessions: a bowling title, a gardening reach game, and a simple balance mini-game package.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the three titles on his latest design deck: the bowling title, the gardening reach game, and a rhythm timing game with better telemetry than the balance package.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Two of the three games overlap, so references to 'the starter set' feel mutually anchored; neither realizes the third game differs because they assume the latest list is already shared.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both assess if the pilot is 'ready for approval' or 'ready to launch.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes readiness means the clinical flow is safe and usable enough to begin with a small cohort, while remaining operational refinements can be patched during early rollout.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes readiness means the pilot package has sufficiently finalized support procedures, onboarding consistency, and reporting definitions so the experience can be replicated without redesign during rollout.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design reviews, saying something is 'ready with minor edits' is common shorthand; because both are collaborative and the remaining issues sound small on the surface, they do not interrogate the threshold behind the same word.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in remote setup
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree patients can be 'set up remotely' after the initial prescription.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes remote setup means a scheduled tele-rehab session where a therapist or assistant watches the patient position sensors, tests motions, and adjusts the game choice live.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes remote setup means patients follow in-app onboarding and auto-calibration on their own, with human support only if the automated flow fails.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are discussing the same high-level objective of not requiring an extra in-person visit, and 'remote setup' is a familiar phrase that hides the distinction between synchronous clinician-guided setup and asynchronous self-serve setup.

turns.inner_thought: I need this review to land on conditional approval today. From my side, the pilot is ready for approval if the clinical flow is workable and safe for a small outpatient cohort next month, even if some of the paperwork and downstream logistics get cleaned up as we go. If this starts sounding too heavy, operations will stall it.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. I’d like to use today to confirm whether this home gaming pilot is ready for a small outpatient launch next month and just identify any final tweaks we need before approval.

turns.inner_thought: The design is close, but I only want to call it ready if the reusable structure is actually settled. We need the starter game set locked as the three titles from my current deck, the remote setup flow defined around the self-serve onboarding and auto-calibration path, and the weekly progress summary nailed down as a standardized report artifact. If we gloss over those now, support burden explodes later.
turns.utterance: From the product side, I think the core design is in good shape. Before we call it ready, I’d like to do one pass on the starter game set, the remote setup flow, and the weekly progress summary.

turns.inner_thought: I’m comfortable with the starter game set because our staff already ran mock sessions with the bowling title, the gardening reach game, and that simple balance mini-game package. Patients tolerated them, and the movement demands mapped well to our shoulder and reach goals. No need to reopen that if we want approval to move.
turns.utterance: I’m comfortable with the starter game set. The clinic team already saw patients tolerate those games well in mock sessions, and the movement patterns line up cleanly with the rehab goals we’ve been targeting.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then we’re aligned on the bowling, gardening, and rhythm titles from the deck. That third title is important because it gives cleaner telemetry and more consistent progression signals for the weekly progress summary than the old balance package would. Glad this sounds settled.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I also like that the starter game set gives us a good spread of progression data, and the third title should make the week-to-week comparisons cleaner.

turns.inner_thought: For the weekly progress summary, therapists do not need a polished dashboard ecosystem. They need a quick weekly readout: did the patient do the prescribed movement practice, how did they tolerate it, and should we keep them on the same games next week. If it gets too elaborate, no one in clinic will use it.
turns.utterance: On the weekly progress summary, what matters most to me is that therapists can get a quick read on whether the prescribed practice is happening and whether the patient stayed engaged enough to keep the same plan for the next week.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and it needs to be standardized so it can be viewed the same way by therapists, patients, and admins across sites. Session completion, calibrated range, and challenge progression should all sit in a comparable weekly progress summary format. If it’s just a therapist note, we lose scalability.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I’d just want the weekly progress summary to be consistent enough that it can be shared across therapists and with patients too, especially around calibration range and challenge progression.

turns.inner_thought: Setup feels manageable because after the initial prescription visit, we can set patients up remotely through the hospital’s usual tele-rehab video workflow. A therapist or assistant can watch the home positioning, verify the adapted motions live, and make sure the game choice is appropriate without bringing them back in person.
turns.utterance: The setup process feels manageable to me because once the prescription visit is done, the patient can be set up remotely, and the therapist can confirm the adapted motions from home.

turns.inner_thought: Right, remote setup should scale because the kit already guides the patient through mobile onboarding and automated calibration on their own. Live support should be the exception, only for failures or unusual cases. That’s the whole point of avoiding a labor-intensive model.
turns.utterance: I think remote setup should scale fine. The kit already walks patients through calibration, so ideally only edge cases would need live help.

turns.inner_thought: As long as therapists screen who is appropriate for this and we carry over standard home-exercise precautions, I’m comfortable describing it as safe for home use. I don’t want to bog the packet down by re-specifying every routine clinical safeguard everyone already uses.
turns.utterance: On safety, I’m comfortable with home use as long as therapists screen appropriate patients and the usual home-program precautions are carried over into the pilot instructions.

turns.inner_thought: I’m fine with home use because the package itself should prevent most foreseeable misuse. Built-in calibration limits, clear onboarding guidance, and obvious fail states mean patients won’t need much clinician intervention after setup. That’s what makes this durable beyond one clinic.
turns.utterance: That sounds right to me. I’m comfortable with home use because the onboarding and controller limits should keep the package safe even without much clinician intervention after setup.

turns.inner_thought: This is enough. From a clinical standpoint, the pilot is ready for approval now, with only minor documentation cleanup. We can patch small wording issues as we go. I want the approval note out this week before anyone starts reopening operational details and delaying the launch.
turns.utterance: So from a clinical standpoint, I’d say the pilot is ready with minor documentation edits. If that works for you, we should finalize the approval note this week.

turns.inner_thought: It’s close enough that I won’t block it, but I still need the launch materials tightened so this can be replicated cleanly: the onboarding notes should reflect the asynchronous remote setup path, and the reporting language should define the weekly progress summary in a standardized way. If I can make those updates now, we preserve structure for the first cohort.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think it’s close to ready. I’ll tighten the onboarding notes and the reporting language so the launch materials are complete for the first cohort.
